stem: A hospital uses a bedside visual cue for clients assessed as high fall risk. What is the most appropriate interpretation of this practice?

options.A: Use the visual cue to help staff recognize fall risk while still using formal assessment and an individualized prevention plan.
options.B: Treat the visual cue as a replacement for fall-risk assessment because the symbol alone determines which prevention measures are needed.
options.C: Interpret the visual cue as a dietary marker because fall risk should not be communicated with bedside reminders for staff.
options.D: Use the visual cue mainly to restrict visitors because limiting family contact is a standard intervention for preventing inpatient falls.

rationale: AHRQ Fall TIPS uses bedside visual tools to communicate patient-specific fall risks and tailored prevention interventions, but the program remains a three-step process of formal risk assessment, personalized prevention planning and consistent execution. Therefore A is correct. B incorrectly replaces assessment with the cue, while C and D misstate the purpose of the bedside tool.
educational_objective: Use bedside fall-risk communication tools as part of—not a substitute for—formal assessment and individualized fall-prevention planning.
source_organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)
source_document_title: Fall TIPS: A Patient-Centered Fall Prevention Toolkit
source_locator: Background and Fall Prevention Toolkit — three-step process: assess fall risk, develop personalized plan, execute consistently; bedside tools communicate patient-specific risks/interventions.
source_claim_supported: Bedside visual tools communicate individualized fall risks/interventions and do not replace formal assessment or tailored planning.

blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — fall prevention and communication to prevent safety events.
